text: Hello, everyone. My name is Jenna Kline, and I'm a post-doc at
MIT.
Today, I'll be giving a lightning talk on KaberTools, a tool
for automated
video-based animal behavioral monitoring.
KaberTools first started as the Kaber
datasets. Kaber stands for the Kenyan Animal
Behavior Recognition from drone videos.
This dataset was collected by myself and a wonderful team of
collaborators over about a month at Impala
Research Center in Laikipia, Kenya, in 2023.
We collected behavior videos of three species,
ended up with about 10 hours of footage, which was processed to
produce over 900 videos with annotated
behavior.
And as of this recording, has been downloaded about
200,000 times on Hugging Face.
Through the annotation process and subsequent data
analysis, we developed our KaberTools,
which is now a modular workflow for
video-based animal behavior monitoring.
Starting with video data collection from either drones or camera
traps, all the way through machine learning-based methods with manual
oversight to process the data through to
ecological analysis.
We provide tips and tricks for dealing with large video
datasets and three main stages of ML
processing,
which consists of three main tasks: detection,
tracking, and behavior annotation.
These computer vision tasks are all model-agnostic.
You can swap out custom behavior recognition models or custom
trackers and choose the degree of autonomy that
is most appropriate for your particular study
system.
And collaborators have used this tool for
camera trap-based and drone-based
studies of African wild dogs.
So a couple of the different ecological research questions KaberTools can
support. One is time budgets.
These tools are designed to extract ecological insight from videos at
scale.
We also provide scripts to automatically calculate behavior
transitions,
look at things like land use and differences in land use
across species,
and
even track individual identities and their characteristic
behavior patterns. In this case, this was used for the African wild
dog study.
